title: Signature generation fails for SM2 private keys with ES256 algorithm for node 18 version
security_topic: support for SM2 keys in JWS/JOSE
qa_summary: Whether SM2 private keys can be used with the ES256 algorithm in this library, with the answer citing the IANA JWS algorithm registry and a Node.js PR.

comments.author: balnenikhil
comments.body:
### Description

`jwt.sign(<payload>, <utf8 encoded SM2 private key>, { algorithm: 'ES256' })` fails with `"error":{"code":"ERR_OSSL_INVALID_DIGEST","library":"Provider routines","reason":"invalid digest"}`  when using node 18.17.0.

The above command works fine with node version 16 but fails with node versions 18 and 20.

### Environment

- **Version of this library used:** jsonwebtoken 9.0.0  and 9.0.2
- **Version of the platform or framework used:** nodejs 18.17.0

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
There is no registered JWS algorithm for SM2 keys[^iana] and ES256 requires the use of an EC key using the P-256 curve. Furthermore Node.js does not fully support SM2 keys.[^node]

Bottom line use of SM2 keys with JOSE is unsupported and out of scope.

[^iana]: https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-algorithms
[^node]: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/37066

title: error:04075070:rsa routines:RSA_sign:digest too big for rsa key
security_topic: RSA key length requirements for JOSE
qa_summary: The developer needed to know the minimum RSA key bit length required for signing tokens, which the answer anchors to the JWA specification.

### Description

I can get HS512 to work, but when I switch to RS512, I get `error:04075070:rsa routines:RSA_sign:digest too big for rsa key`. I get the same error whether using RS256 or RS512.

### Reproduction

My code is this:

```
const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");

const token = jwt.sign({ sub: 1 }, "...", { expiresIn: '7d', algorithm: "RS512" });
```

### Environment

- **Version of this library used:** 8.5.1
- **Version of the platform or framework used, if applicable:**
- **Other relevant versions (language, server software, OS, browser):** Node in Windows
- **Other modules/plugins/libraries that might be involved:** express-jwt

comments.body:
Your RSA key is of insufficient bit length. 2048 bits is minimum required by the JWA specification.

Furthermore, don't sign with HS* using an RSA key :)

title: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`
security_topic: default algorithm verification for JWT 'none' algorithm
qa_summary: Whether the verify function defaults to accepting all algorithms including 'none', with the answer referencing issue #711 as the duplicate for the requirement of explicitly allowing 'none'.

comments.author: daniel-j-h
comments.body:
By default `sign` uses `options.algorithm: "HS256"`.

In contrast `verify` does not use `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]` by default - but instead accepts all algorithms.

This means by default we sign with HS256 but we verify and accept all algorithms - for example also the `none` algorithm.

If we're setting a default in sign we should set the same default in verify - and keep them in sync.

Thoughts?

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
source: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/v8.5.1/verify.js#L99-L118

> but instead accepts all algorithms

That is a false statement.

Verify's `algorithm` option default value is derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument value and it never defaults to accepting **all algorithms**. The accidental acceptance of `none` tokens is **also prevented**.

What lead you this expectation of accepting everything?

comments.author: daniel-j-h
comments.body:
Here is an example of what I mean. Create a token with algorithm none

```js
> jwt.sign({ user: 42 }, undefined, { algorithm: 'none' });
'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.'
```

The key is not needed - I set it to undefined.

By default now we can verify that token without having to explicitly allow none as an algorithm

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.')
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

and also works in this scenario when we accidentally pass undefined (or anything else false-y as an argument)

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.', process.env.MYKEY) // oops env var undefined
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

It would be best if we could make this explicit - the user should pass `algorithms: ["none"]` if the user really knows what this means and implies.

This is the case for all algorithm options. By default sign sets `HS256` as an algorithm but in verify by default we accept all algorithms e.g. we also accept a token signed with `HS512`.

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
> but instead accepts all algorithms

so, this is not true.

For the `none` being explicitly required as algorithms option we already have #711 as duplicate.

For the rest, accepting HS512 when you, by default, sign with HS256 isn't that big of a deal. However, we think that in general defaulting to use HS256 even when a private key value is passed in is a problem in itself and will be changing that for next major too, so that the algorithm is derived of the `secretOrPrivateKey` argument same as for verify today.

title: RFC confrontation on "none" algo
security_topic: acceptance of unsigned JWTs with 'none' algorithm
qa_summary: Whether the library's acceptance of the 'none' algorithm in JWTs is a security risk and if it aligns with RFC 7518, which the maintainer addresses by referencing the project's source code and the RFC.

comments.author: frankli0324
comments.body:
### Description

According to https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7518#section-3.6, jws s "MUST NOT accept such objects as valid unless the application specifies that it is acceptable for a specific object to not be integrity protected"

### Reproduction

```javascript
> var token = jwt.sign({'a':1}, 'asdf', { algorithm: 'none'})
undefined
> jwt.verify(token)
{ a: 1, iat: 1587359376 }
```

maybe we should add some kind of switch options?

### Expected output:

```javascript
> var token = jwt.sign({'a':1}, 'asdf', { algorithm: 'none'})
undefined
> jwt.verify(token)
throws error
> jwt.verify(token, '', { algorithm: 'none'})
{ a: 1, iat: 1587359376 }
```

comments.author: frankli0324
comments.body:
https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/5f10bf9957a2541828501cfecab0310908b2f62f/verify.js#L109-L111

so it's intentional?

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
@frankli0324 `none` won't be automatically accepted unless the developer provided no `keyOrSecret`. The three lines in isolation aren't the whole story.

https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/5f10bf9957a2541828501cfecab0310908b2f62f/verify.js#L101-L118

comments.author: frankli0324
comments.body: from my point of view, providing no secret doesn't mean that one explicitly "specifies that it is acceptable for a specific object to not be integrity protected", more like a mistake one could jump into

comments.author: panva
comments.body: We'll consider making the `algorithms` option required when accepting unsigned JWTs for the next major.

title: Less Secure (jwt token decodes without any secret)
security_topic: JWT signing vs encryption
qa_summary: The developer needed to know if JWT tokens are encrypted for confidentiality and the answer references the JWT structure documentation from Auth0 and RFC 7519.

comments.author: yacineMTB
comments.body:
`jwt.sign` is for signing a token, not encrypting it. With signing, you use a private key to sign a message so that a consumer of the message can use a public key (or the private key, depending if you chose a symmetric algorithm to sign the payload) to verify its authenticity.

For more information; check out [this document](https://auth0.com/docs/tokens/references/jwt-structure). 
Also, [this RFC](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519) specifies the JSON web token standard, as well as what some JWT claims are used for.

Hope this helps!

comments.author: jhiner
comments.body: To add to @yacineMTB 's response, you can decode a token without verifying its signature. This is why you see this behavior with jwt.io. This distinction is referenced in the readme here: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken#jwtdecodetoken--options

comments.author: panva
comments.body:

title: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)
security_topic: ignoring JWT signature verification for testing
qa_summary: The developer wanted to know if they could safely ignore JWT signature verification for testing, and the maintainer answered concretely by linking to the verify.js source at commit a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c where the option could be added.

comments.author: rockebee
comments.body:
### Describe the problem you'd like to have solved

> In dev and test environments it may be feasible to work with a test JWT token which has no valid signature, e. g. for cases where the token provider can not be modified to create tokens in a manner how a relying party needs it for a special edge situation. In this case the JWT payload could be modified manually be the developer to match/test the requirement, but the current jsonwebtoken implementation does not allow to use this invalid token within ```jwt.verify()``` function.

### Describe the ideal solution

> Adding a new option ```ignoreSignature``` to the existing set of options (like ```ignoreExpiration``` and ```ignoreNotBefore```) would allow developers to use self-modified tokens for tests but still having checks for proper ```issuer```, ```subject```, ```audience``` in place.

## Alternatives and current work-arounds

> Using of ```jwt.decode()``` instead of ```jwt.verify()``` helps in at least getting the JWT decoded properly, but as mentioned above does not allow for getting other verification checks run (```issuer``` etc.)

### Additional context

> no additional input here

comments.author: rockebee
comments.body:
One more note: From looking into source code it should be easy to get implemented by modifying ```verify.js``` somewhere around here: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c/verify.js#L126-L134

If you are interested, I could try to prepare a PR for this.

comments.author: ziluvatar
comments.body:
I think it is too risky to add that option to the `verify()` function, without signature the rest of checks do not make sense, you can not trust the information you got. Also I think they key point is here:
> for a special edge situation

I'd say to try to solve that special edge case by fixing the interoperability between both.

Other possible workarounds:
* You could mock the Token Provider depending on your tests.
* You can build an abstraction using `.decode()` as you said in testing, really... any other check without signature verification can be forced to fail whenever you want.
  * Even that abstraction could do `decode()` + `sign()` another token with same payload and `none` algorithm or use one secret for testing an use one of `HS` algorithms + `verify()`.

Anyway whatever you do it has the risk to end up running in production due to a misconfiguration. 😅 

PS: Nice way to present your request 👏

# Backport Request: SSRF Vulnerability (CVE-2025-62718) to 0.x branch

## Description

A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability has been identified in axios, assigned CVE-2025-62718. This vulnerability has been fixed in the 1.x branch but is still present in the 0.x branch, which is still widely used.

## Request

I kindly request consideration for backporting the fix for this vulnerability to the 0.x branch to ensure the security of users still relying on this version.

## Rationale

1. Security: SSRF vulnerabilities can lead to severe security issues, allowing attackers to make unauthorized requests from the server.
2. Legacy Version Support: Many projects still use the 0.x branch and may not be ready to upgrade to 1.x for various reasons.
3. Security Compliance: Backporting this fix will help projects using 0.x meet security requirements.

## Additional Information

- CVE: CVE-2025-62718
- Fixed in branch: 1.15.0
- Backport needed to: 0.x

Thank you for considering this request. If any additional information or assistance is needed in the backporting process, please let me know.

title: Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise
security_topic: circumvention of 2FA via RAT
qa_summary: How to identify and remediate the axios npm supply chain compromise, with remediation steps anchored to specific malicious versions (1.14.1 and 0.30.4) and external technical analyses from StepSecurity, Snyk, and Socket.

comments.author: jasonsaayman
comments.body:
# Post Mortem: axios npm supply chain compromise

**Date:** March 31, 2026
**Author:** Jason Saayman
**Status:** Remediation in progress

On March 31, 2026, two malicious versions of axios (1.14.1 and 0.30.4) were published to the npm registry through my compromised account. Both versions injected a dependency called `plain-crypto-js@4.2.1` that installed a remote access trojan on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

The malicious versions were live for about 3 hours before being removed.

## Are you affected?

Check your lockfile:
```bash
grep -E "axios@(1\.14\.1|0\.30\.4)|plain-crypto-js" package-lock.json yarn.lock 2>/dev/null
```
If anything comes back, treat that machine as compromised:
1. Downgrade to `axios@1.14.0` (or `0.30.3` for 0.x users)
2. Delete `node_modules/plain-crypto-js/`
3. Rotate every secret, token, and credential on that machine
4. Check your network logs for connections to `sfrclak[.]com` or `142.11.206.73` on port 8000
5. If this happened on a CI runner, rotate any secrets that were injected during the affected build

If you were already pinned to a clean version and didn't run a fresh install between 00:21 and 03:15 UTC on March 31, you're fine.

For detailed remediation guidance, including CI/CD-specific steps, see:
- [StepSecurity: full technical analysis and remediation](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan)
- [Snyk: advisory and scanning guidance](https://snyk.io/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-supply-chain-attack-delivers-cross-platform/)
- [Socket: Supply Chain Attack on Axios Pulls Malicious Dependency from npm](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised)

## What happened

The attacker gained access to the lead maintainer's PC through a targeted social engineering campaign and RAT malware. This gave them access to the npm account credentials, which they used to publish the malicious versions.

The attack followed patterns documented in similar campaigns targeting open source maintainers.

## Resolution

Complete wipe of all lead maintainer devices as well as resetting of all credentials. This includes all accounts irrespective of platform, both personal and all other capacities.

## What's changing

To prevent this from happening again, these are the changes being made:

| Action | Type |
| --- | --- |
| Reset of all devices and credentials | Prevention |
| Immutable release setup | Prevention |
| Proper adoption of OIDC flow for publishing | Prevention |
| Improvement of overall security posture | Prevention |
| Updating of all GitHub actions to adopt best practices | Prevention |

This list is not the end. We will continue actively working on improving security beyond these items.

## Attack Timeline

I don't have an exact timeline for when the initial compromise occurred, but this is the sequence of events for the package itself:
- About 2 weeks before March 31: social engineering campaign initiated against the lead maintainer
- March 30, 05:57 UTC: `plain-crypto-js@4.2.0` published to npm
- March 31, 00:21 UTC: `axios@1.14.1` published with `plain-crypto-js@4.2.1` injected
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: `axios@0.30.4` published with the same payload
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: first external detections
- March 31, around 01:00 UTC: community members file issues reporting the compromise. The attacker deletes them using the compromised account.
- March 31, 01:38 UTC: axios collaborator DigitalBrainJS opens PR #10591 to deprecate the compromised versions, flags the deleted issues to the community, and contacts npm directly
- March 31, 03:15 UTC: malicious versions removed from npm
- March 31, 03:29 UTC: `plain-crypto-js` removed from npm

For detailed technical timelines:
- [StepSecurity: forensic timeline](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan)
- [Datadog Security Labs: full attack flow and response analysis](https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/)


## Lessons learned

We are actively investigating how unauthorized access was obtained and reviewing all aspects of our security posture and access controls. While we do not have confirmed details to share at this time, this incident reinforces the need for continuous monitoring, strong account protections, and vigilance across both project infrastructure and individual maintainer environments.

We will continue to strengthen our practices in alignment with industry best practices and in collaboration with groups such as the OpenJS Security Working Group.

Security posture should be continuously monitored and improved. Specifically from this incident:

- Publishing directly from a personal account was a risk that could have been avoided. The OIDC flow and immutable release setup we are now adopting should have been in place before this happened.
- There was no automated way to detect an unauthorized publish. Detection depended entirely on the community noticing.
- Open source maintainers with high-impact packages are active targets for sophisticated social engineering. Hyper vigilance is needed both on the registry and in a personal capacity.


## Summary for broarder audience

We can confirm that two compromised versions of Axios were briefly made available through a widely used software download system due to unauthorized access to the lead maintainer's account, not a change to the underlying code.

We are working with the companies that operate this system, along with security experts, to investigate and contain the issue. Organizations that installed these versions should remove them immediately and treat affected systems as potentially compromised, including rotating any sensitive credentials.

This was the result of a compromised lead maintainer's account, and we are actively investigating how access was obtained. We do not have confirmed details to share at this time.


## Acknowledgments

Thanks to @DigitalBrainJS for acting fast when the compromised account had higher permissions than his own and for getting npm to take action. Thanks to Open Source Community and the npm security team for their fast response.

The malicious versions have been removed from npm and are no longer infecting users. The immediate incident is resolved. We are actively working on the security improvements listed above to prevent this from happening again.

I'll update this as the investigation progresses. Questions welcome in this thread.

comments.author: feross
comments.body:
Thanks for the thorough post-mortem, Jason. Writing one of these is never easy, and the transparency here is exactly what the ecosystem needs.

A few things worth highlighting for others reading this:

The response was fast. ~3 hours from publish to removal is a good outcome given the constraints. @DigitalBrainJS in particular deserves recognition for acting decisively.

For maintainers of high-download packages, this incident reinforces a few things we'd recommend:

1. OIDC-based publishing (provenance attestation) is the single highest-leverage change you can make. It removes long-lived credentials from the equation entirely. Glad to see this is on the roadmap.
2. Publish from CI, not from a local machine. If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.
3. Enable npm's mandatory 2FA for publish, and use a hardware key if possible. TOTP on a compromised machine is not 2FA.

We detected the malicious `axios@1.14.1` and `axios@0.30.4` versions within minutes of publication and blocked it for users with the [AI Detected Potential Malware](https://socket.dev/alerts/gptMalware) alert enabled. Thanks for sharing our [analysis](https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised). 

This kind of targeted social engineering against individual maintainers is the new normal. It's not a reflection on Jason or the axios team -- these campaigns are sophisticated and persistent. We're seeing them across the ecosystem and they're only accelerating.

Wishing you and the team the best as you work through the remaining security work here. The npm ecosystem is better for having maintainers who respond like this.

  - sadly, most CI & MCP tooling setup docs, always advise to simply run: `npx <package>@latest`
- check the network logs in your CI during those times. 
- `npx` call hardening with pre-install + lock file generation + using `--no --offline`
  - full technical details here: https://socket.dev/blog/hidden-blast-radius-of-the-axios-compromise

comments.author: shaanmajid
comments.body:
@feross

>OIDC-based publishing (provenance attestation) is the single highest-leverage change you can make. It removes long-lived credentials from the equation entirely. Glad to see this is on the roadmap.
Publish from CI, not from a local machine. If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.
Enable npm's mandatory 2FA for publish, and use a hardware key if possible. TOTP on a compromised machine is not 2FA.

Worth noting that Axios was already following most of these recommendations, and it still wasn't enough to prevent this compromise.

The v1.x publish workflow has had provenance since 2023. The last four legitimate v1 releases (1.13.4 through 1.14.0) all went through GitHub Actions with Trusted Publishing. You can verify this via the [registry data](https://registry.npmjs.org/axios): each was published with Trusted Publishing and provenance attestations. The malicious v1.14.1 has neither. I have a brief summary of the registry evidence [here](https://gist.github.com/shaanmajid/fa1bb71f063476f3e8fa726f54fd2d37). (There was a stray `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` in the v1 publish workflow at the time of compromise, removed in #10619, but it wasn't doing anything for the last few releases; OIDC was correctly set up and the OIDC token was overriding it.)

(v0.x never had a CI publish workflow and was always published locally. That wasn't great, but it also isn't why the compromise happened. The attacker had RAT access and published directly to the registry, bypassing CI entirely.)

@jasonsaayman confirmed elsewhere that he had 2FA enabled on all accounts, including GitHub and npm.

I'd still recommend all projects use Trusted Publishing and attestations, but that alone clearly wasn't enough here. The core problem is this part of your reply (emphasis mine):

> Publish from CI, not from a local machine. **If a maintainer's laptop is compromised, the blast radius shouldn't include the ability to push a release.**

As things stand, **nothing** on npmjs can be configured to enforce this. The strictest package-level setting npm offers maintainers in their package publication settings -- "Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens (recommended)" -- does not block local `npm publish`. It opens a  browser window for 2FA, but with a RAT on the machine and software-based TOTP, that's trivial to circumvent (as you noted). There is no npmjs setting to require OIDC-only publishing, unlike some other registries, e.g., crates.io.

I commend Axios's commitment towards improving their supply-chain security -- all projects have gaps, and it requires constant vigilance to resolve them -- but I think the only mitigation on Axios's end that could have actually prevented this would have been using hardware FIDO2 keys for maintainer's npm auth, which can't be hijacked by a RAT.

The bigger gaps are elsewhere IMO:
- npmjs (and other registries) should allow packages to opt in to OIDC-only publishing rejecting all non-OIDC publishes at the registry level.
- [Dependency cooldown periods](https://blog.yossarian.net/2025/11/21/We-should-all-be-using-dependency-cooldowns): the malicious versions were live for ~3 hours. A mere 3-day cooldown would never have pulled them. Dependabot, Renovate, uv, and bun all support `minimumReleaseAge` or   equivalent.
- Consumers and tooling should verify attestations: every legitimate v1 release had OIDC provenance; the malicious one didn't. Any tool checking for this would have flagged it instantly. But provenance verification is opt-in, and practically nobody does it today.

comments.author: DanielRuf
comments.body:
@aeneasr please provide rules for YARA or Sigma. These are the default tools to scan for IOCs.

@tayvano I have nothing to add. You are right and I'm getting warnings about these threat actors for a very long time.

The only thing I want to add: please always put secrets in some secure password / secrets vault with a very strong passphrase. Don't trust people you don't know. And use separate devices / laptops for different tasks (meeting vs work). I know people who got hacked just because they had only one device for everything.

Not going to suggest building some scenarios with MITRE ATT&CK, but please apply some defense in depth and zero-trust or human-in-the-loop solutions.

In the Trivy and LiteLLM cases I recommended for example Shamirs Secret Sharing or in general splitting secrets between multiple persons. Sure, that won't help much when only one person works on the project. But most secrets just wait there to be taken and nothing prevents that when some malware exfiltrates the content of your home folder. Secrets can always be sharded (even offline) or moved to some hardware key for a very long time (Windows for example had the boot disks as a first defense against maiden attacks, but this is a different story).

Not sure if I will build some solution, but plaintext secret sharding can be done offline with a very simple and cheap solution: nfc chips (as stickers) that you can place in different rooms and scanned in the right order give you the full secret.

Not going to name specific free / paid solutions for secrets vaults, but you can always seal them in a separate location and with a minimum number of shards - one per relevant person. This is already done in practice for money vaults and other very critical things (rockets for example too). A single compromised user / device should not lead to full takeover.

Edit: I always recommend blameless post mortems and I'm a strong proponent of sharing lessons learned, working on solutions together.

If there is some interest to create some Security WG, I can help with that @jasonsaayman (https://github.com/nodejs/security-wg?tab=readme-ov-file#emeritus-members, https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm-security-wg). I'm open to provide any help you need, people like @tayvano have probably a great overview and understanding of such threats and how defenders have to adapt to it.

comments.author: DanielRuf
comments.body:
@SerJaimeLannister well, social engineering like in offline red teaming scenarios is basically testing, how much you trust other random people.

Technical solutions can help only partly, and do not always prevent all damages.

I can probably name more cases from work. But as @tayvano made clear, professional threat actors like nationstate actors quickly adapt their strategy. This is more about how you think when you are under pressure or alone. The xz incident was planned much longer and they gained the trust of the sole maintainer there.

Package cooldown settings, OIDC and more only cover specific things. But without any package vetting happening for new releases on npmjs, there is not much trust. We had a time with GPG where the web of trust was important. And npmjs had used GPG signatures in the background. We would need something like that for registries. If @feross and other trusted parties sign with their GPG key, that a release would be "ok", you can safely install it. But GPG was never meant to scale that much and npm was never designed for this. Not saying WOT is useless. But maintainers fail, what is left to stop you from installing a new release? Do you take a look at https://app.unpkg.com/axios@1.14.0 or some other solution, before you actually download something? Do you remember to set `ignore-scripts` on new devices?

My proposal is to gather people who can push security of the whole developer ecosystem. Otherwise these will be always isolated cases and the next incident with a different package with no or less security measures (technical & organizational) will hit people again.

As you can see there, it's not that easy when you count all possible techniques and tactics with social engineering / phishing mentioned:
https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/enterprise/
https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/enterprise/

There are good reasons, why deno (from the Nodejs creator) strictly requires you to provide the allowed permissions (like network, I/O, ...). Most developers will still have most credentials in one place / environment and as long as insecure defaults like `ignore-scripts` or long-lived tokens are there, those who are not aware of the risks will still fall victim. And qubesos would not be an option for those (also most do not want to and can not change their OS or install extra software). So either registries or tool providers (npm, npmjs, GitHub) or maintainers have to work on the solutions, that protect everyone by default.

comments.author: tayvano
comments.body:
**Regarding 2FA questions that keep coming up...**

2FA protects the login step—the initial authentication. 2FA is important—mandatory imo. Because it protects against your username/password being leaked and a lot of phishing.

But how it works is that once you are authenticated, the platforms issue a session token/cookie which is stored on your device or in your browser and is used for future authentication. If you think about it, it's obvious. You don't have to 2FA every time you make a call to npm or github. This is why.

When you have a RAT on your device, it grabs your post-authentication state, making 2FA irrelevant.

Here's some places we know they exfiltrate:

- `.aws`
- `.azure`
- `.bit/config`
- `.cargo/credentials`
- `.circleci/cli.yml`
- `.config/configstore/firebase-tools.json`
- `.config/doctl/config.yaml`
- `.config/gcloud`
- `.config/gh`
- `.config/glab-cli`
- `.config/linode-cli`
- `.config/stripe/config.toml`
- `.gem/credentials`
- `.netfily`
- `.netrc`
- `.npmrc` (long-lived bearer token)
- `.nuget/NuGet.Config`
- `.oci`
- `.pulumi/credentials.json`
- `.pypirc`
- `.twilio-cli`
- `.vault-token`
- `.vercel`
- `.wrangler/config`
- `.yarnrc.yml`
- your entire keychain
- all your password managers and everything inside
- all your browser storage, cookies, autofills, passwords, and history

Issuing short and long lived authentication tokens is standard operating procedure for every single platform and product you use. It's why you don't have to login and enter MFA every time you click a link, make a call, etc. The information to authenticate lives on your device.

This obviously becomes a problem when the attackers have a backdoor to your device and why 2FA will not protect you in this situation.

comments.author: DigitalBrainJS
comments.body:
If npm had a cool-down period during which it publishes a version that can only be installed manually using a special tag, support for one-time kill switch tokens (in our context, we'd call them quarantine tokens) with the optional publish webhook, such attacks would be almost impossible, even if a group of North Korean hackers were sitting at the PC of an npm package admin. 
In addition to manual activation of the token by one of the maintainers in case something bad happened, they could also add an external watcher with an algorithmic and possibly AI analyzer, and such an attack would be nipped in the bud. 
Nothing bad would happen in case of false-positive token activation, due to which maintainers won't be able to publish new versions, and users will not be able to install the very latest versions for a couple of days, but very bad things happen when maintainers lose control of a package, even for a few hours.
In this particular attack, we lost 40-50 minutes because there was no way to block the packet distribution ourselves.

comments.author: Jeremitc
comments.body:
> I've started a discussion for npm to add password/2FA confirmation for sensitive changes like email, token creation etc
> 
> https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/191503
> 
> Right now, as long as you're logged in to npm, an attacker can do anything, which is pretty bad.

Absolutely agree. The recent Axios incident (#10636) highlights exactly why this is a critical missing piece in NPM's security architecture. The reliance purely on an active session cookie without an escalation challenge for sensitive actions is an unacceptable risk given the modern threat landscape, where AI-assisted social engineering, fake interviews, and infostealers are extremely common.

To actually help prevent these supply chain attacks moving forward, NPM desperately needs a Sudo Mode (similar to what GitHub already implements natively).

I suggest the community pushes for the following features to be implemented:

Strict Re-Authentication Challenge: Require re-entering a password, 2FA code, or WebAuthn/Passkey confirmation specifically for sensitive actions:
Creating, modifying or deleting Automation/Access Tokens.
Adding or removing package maintainers/owners.
Changing the primary email or security settings.
Session Isolation: Just because someone stole an active session cookie to browse logged in, doesn't mean they should have the authority to publish code or create tokens without passing a physical hardware check (like a YubiKey or Passkey) in that exact moment.
We need to support this request aggressively. A successful phishing attack on a single developer should never be enough to automatically compromise millions of machines downstream. It's time for NPM to upgrade their session management logic!

title: DeprecationWarning: url.parse() used in proxy resolution → Node DEP0169
security_topic: migration from deprecated url.parse to WHATWG URL API
qa_summary: Whether the use of the deprecated url.parse() API in proxy resolution poses security risks and which PR (pull request #7499) fixes this by migrating to the WHATWG URL API.

comments.author: vamsee9
comments.body:
DeprecationWarning: `url.parse()` used during Axios proxy resolution in Node (DEP0169)

When using Axios v1.13.2 in a Node/SSR environment, Axios triggers Node’s deprecation warning for `url.parse()`:

```
(node:XXXX) [DEP0169] DeprecationWarning: `url.parse()` behavior is not standardized and prone to errors that have security implications. Use the WHATWG URL API instead.
```

The stack trace consistently points to Axios’ internal proxy resolution path:

```
at urlParse (node:url:136:13)
at Object.getProxyForUrl (node_modules/proxy-from-env/index.js:…)
at setProxy (node_modules/axios/lib/…)
at dispatchHttpRequest (...)
```

This happens whenever Axios runs in Node with proxy support enabled (via HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY / NO_PROXY env vars or Axios proxy configuration). The `proxy-from-env` package used internally still depends on `url.parse()`, which Node has deprecated under DEP0169.

Reproduction:

* Node.js v18+ or v20+
* Axios v1.13.2
* Any SSR environment (Next.js, Express, server functions)
* Proxy environment variables set, or Axios configured with `proxy: true`
* Execute any Axios request; Node logs DEP0169

Impact:

* Logs are polluted with deprecation warnings in SSR workloads
* `url.parse()` is flagged for removal in future Node versions
* Continued dependency on deprecated URL parsing introduces compliance and security concerns
* No configuration currently exists to disable proxy resolution or switch Axios to WHATWG URL internally

Expected:

* Axios should use WHATWG `URL` instead of `url.parse()` inside proxy resolution
* Proxy detection should avoid deprecated APIs
* No DEP0169 warnings in modern Node runtimes

Suggested fix:

* Replace `url.parse()` usage inside Axios’ proxy path with `new URL()`
* Update or wrap `proxy-from-env` with a WHATWG-safe implementation
* Provide a configuration flag such as `proxyResolve: false` or `disableProxyEnv: true` to bypass the proxy resolver entirely

Additional context:

* Warning originates from Node’s DEP0169 (WHATWG URL migration)
* SSR frameworks such as Next.js surface this prominently during server rendering
* This issue is reproducible in clean Node environments with Axios alone

Please review and advise whether this deprecation migration is planned, or if a proxy-layer abstraction is being refactored to use the WHATWG URL API.

title: Consider adopting npm trusted publishing
security_topic: adoption of npm trusted publishing for supply chain security
qa_summary: Whether the project should adopt npm trusted publishing to mitigate supply chain risks, with the answer providing a link to the official npm trusted publishing documentation.

comments.author: JamieMagee
comments.body:
Recent [supply chain attacks on npm](https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/our-plan-for-a-more-secure-npm-supply-chain/) have highlighted the need for stronger package publishing security. The September 2025 Shai-Hulud worm compromised 500+ packages through stolen maintainer tokens, showing the risks of token-based publishing.

Trusted publishing helps by eliminating long-lived tokens that can be stolen or accidentally exposed; generating automatic provenance provides cryptographic proof of where/how packages are built; and is an industry standard adopted by PyPI, RubyGems, crates.io, NuGet, etc.

Here's the short version:

1. [Configure a trusted publisher on npmjs.com](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers#github-actions-configuration)
1. Add `id-token: write` permission to your workflow
1. Remove `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN` from your workflow

npm is [planning to deprecate legacy tokens](https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/our-plan-for-a-more-secure-npm-supply-chain/#h-npm-s-roadmap-for-hardening-package-publication) and make trusted publishing the preferred method.

Would you consider adopting trusted publishing to help secure the npm ecosystem?

References:

- [npm trusted publishing documentation](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers)
- [Announcement blog post](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-07-31-npm-trusted-publishing-with-oidc-is-generally-available/)
- [Provenance statements guide](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements)

comments.author: jonchurch
comments.body: You also need to ensure that the package is set to require 2fa to publish, if not published via OIDC. 2fa on your account is one step, but you **must** ensure that the package itself cannot be published with a token. That means you only allow yourself to either publish via OIDC, or w/ 2fa when publishing locally. I know that you have/had this npm setting off, because your [current CI workflow](https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/e2bed7f84d86e87d0641bc5910e96607092d9934/.github/workflows/publish.yml#L31) would not work without it.

spider-yamet
comments.body:
Hello @DigitalBrainJS, @jasonsaayman, @JustinBeckwith Hope you are doing great!
Based on my research, I think this issue is still existing on this codebase, I hope to resolve this issue and let me suggest my approach for this and please let me know if I can proceed with this issue resolving.


## Executive Summary

**Issue**: POST requests with `auth` configuration that receive 303 redirects fail with 401 Unauthorized when using `follow-redirects >= 1.15.8`.

**Status**: This is a **valid axios issue** that needs to be fixed in axios, despite follow-redirects marking the related issue as "invalid". The follow-redirects maintainers' decision actually confirms that axios should handle preserving its own configuration during redirects.

**Proposed Solution**: Preserve the `auth` option during redirects using the existing `beforeRedirects` mechanism, following the same pattern already used for proxy authentication.

---

## Why This Issue Still Exists and Needs Fixing

### 1. Follow-Redirects Marked It as "Invalid" - This Confirms It's an Axios Issue

When follow-redirects maintainers marked [issue #277](https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/issues/277) as "invalid", they were indicating:

- ✅ **Not a bug in follow-redirects** - The library is working as designed
- ✅ **Expected behavior** - follow-redirects handles redirects, but consuming libraries (like axios) should preserve their own configuration
- ✅ **Axios responsibility** - Axios should use the `beforeRedirect` hook to preserve axios-specific options like `auth`

**This is actually evidence that axios needs to fix this**, not a reason to ignore it.

### 2. User Confirmation: Problem Persists

The original reporter ([atjchen](https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/6929)) confirmed on June 16, 2025 that the issue **still exists** even with follow-redirects >= 1.15.8:

> "I still have the problem if i add in package.json: (version >= 1.15.8)"

This demonstrates:
- The issue is real and reproducible
- It affects real users
- Current workarounds (pinning to 1.15.7) are not sustainable long-term

### 3. Code Analysis: Inconsistency in Current Implementation

**Location**: `lib/adapters/http.js`

**The Problem**: 
- ✅ Proxy authentication IS preserved during redirects- uses `beforeRedirects.proxy`
- ❌ Regular authentication is NOT preserved (missing implementation)
- This creates an **inconsistent user experience** - same mechanism, different outcome

**Root Cause**:
- Auth is passed to follow-redirects initially
- But `beforeRedirects` doesn't store it
- `dispatchBeforeRedirect` doesn't restore it 

### 4. Technical Root Cause

When `follow-redirects` processes a redirect (especially 303 See Other):
1. Axios passes `auth` initially
2. follow-redirects calls `beforeRedirect` hook with new options
3. **Missing**: `dispatchBeforeRedirect` doesn't restore the `auth` option
4. **Result**: Redirected request lacks authentication → 401 Unauthorized

---

## Proposed Solution

**Follow the existing proxy pattern** to ensure consistency.

**File**: `lib/adapters/http.js`

**Step 1**: Store auth in `beforeRedirects`
- Add `auth` to `beforeRedirects` object (similar to how proxy is stored)

**Step 2**: Restore auth in `dispatchBeforeRedirect`
- Check if `beforeRedirects.auth` exists and restore it if missing

### Why This Solution Works

1. ✅ **Follows Existing Pattern**: Uses the same mechanism as proxy auth preservation
2. ✅ **Minimal Changes**: Only 2 small code additions
3. ✅ **Backward Compatible**: Doesn't break existing functionality
4. ✅ **Handles Edge Cases**: Checks if auth exists before restoring

title: Axios ignoring allowAbsoluteUrls configuration parameter
security_topic: bypass of absolute URL restriction
qa_summary: Whether the allowAbsoluteUrls configuration parameter was being ignored, potentially allowing requests to absolute URLs (SSRF risk), and the fix is provided in PR #6810 and #6814, with a fixed version of 1.8.3.

comments.author: david-arien
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Starting from Axios v1.8.0, the `allowAbsoluteUrls` attribute was introduced in the configuration to control the use of absolute URLs. (PR: https://github.com/axios/axios/pull/6795)

Currently, this parameter is being ignored in the `buildFullPath` call from the HTTP adapter.

https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/72acf759373ef4e211d5299818d19e50e08c02f8/lib/adapters/http.js#L231

This oversight means that it is still possible to make requests to absolute URLs even when the `allowAbsoluteUrls` configuration attribute is set to `false`.

### Proof of Concept:

Even though `getUri` returns a URL from `example.com`, the request is sent to `evil.com`

```javascript
> const axios = require('axios');
> axios.VERSION
'1.8.1'
> const client = axios.create({baseURL: 'http://example.com/', allowAbsoluteUrls: false});
> client.getUri({url: 'http://evil.com'});
'http://example.com/http://evil.com'
> client.get('http://evil.com');
```

### Solution:

Include the `allowAbsoluteUrls` parameter in the call to the `buildFullPath` function.

https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/72acf759373ef4e211d5299818d19e50e08c02f8/lib/adapters/http.js#L231

```javascript
const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url, config.allowAbsoluteUrls);
```

### To Reproduce

_No response_

### Code snippet

```js
const axios = require('axios');
const client = axios.create({baseURL: 'http://example.com/', allowAbsoluteUrls: false});
client.get('http://evil.com');
```

### Expected behavior

The request should be to example.com

### Axios Version

1.8.0

### Adapter Version

http

title: AxiosHeaders doesn't handle multiple headers returned via fetch adapter
security_topic: Axios header parsing of fetch response
qa_summary: How AxiosHeaders should aggregate multiple Set-Cookie headers without overwriting, answered by citing Node.js HTTP header behavior (Node.js docs: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#messageheaders).

comments.author: panta82
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

When using fetch adapter in node.js, axios iterates over headers by using `header.entries()` (https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/c96aa6257f5a060fedac27ae424486acd3ee705f/lib/core/AxiosHeaders.js#L104).

Headers from fetch will be in this format:
```
[
  [
    "access-control-allow-credentials",
    "true"
  ],
  [
    "access-control-allow-origin",
    ""
  ],
  [
    "connection",
    "keep-alive"
  ],
  [
    "content-length",
    "1991"
  ],
  [
    "content-type",
    "application/json; charset=utf-8"
  ],
  [
    "date",
    "Tue, 01 Oct 2024 15:49:38 GMT"
  ],
  [
    "keep-alive",
    "timeout=5"
  ],
  [
    "set-cookie",
    "test-name1=test-token1; path=/; httponly"
  ],
  [
    "set-cookie",
    "test-name2=test-token2; path=/; httponly"
  ],
  [
    "vary",
    "Origin, Accept-Encoding"
  ]
]
```

Note that there are 2 cookies set. However, axios will overwrite the first cookie with the second one.

I presume it's expecting to get cookies in an array form. But fetch adapter returns a raw list.

### To Reproduce

https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/optimistic-worker-mx8tcx?file=%2Findex.js

My output:
```
with http adapter [ 'a=x; Path=/', 'b=y; Path=/' ]
with fetch adapter b=y; Path=/
```

### Code snippet

```js
import axiosLib from "axios";

const axios1 = axiosLib.create({adapter: 'http', maxRedirects: 0, validateStatus: () => true}); 
const resp1 = await axios1.get("http://httpbin.org/cookies/set?a=x&b=y");
console.log('with http adapter', resp1.headers['set-cookie']);

const axios2 = axiosLib.create({adapter: 'fetch', maxRedirects: 0, validateStatus: () => true}); 
const resp2 = await axios2.get("http://httpbin.org/cookies/set?a=x&b=y", {
    fetchOptions: {
        redirect: 'manual'
    }
});
console.log('with fetch adapter', resp2.headers['set-cookie']);
```


### Expected behavior

Fetch adapter should reorganize headers so they are in node.js format, where repeated headers are collected.

### Axios Version

1.7.7

### Adapter Version

bundled fetch

### Browser

_No response_

### Browser Version

_No response_

### Node.js Version

v20.12.1

### OS

linux

comments.author: panta82
comments.body:
In node.js, I think the rule is:

for all headers:
- for the first occurance -> set as `'h1=v1'`
- for the second occurrence -> convert to `['h1=v1', 'h2=v2']`

for `set-cookie`:
- for the first occurrence -> set as `['h1=v1']`
- for the second occurrence -> append to existing list `['h1=v1', 'h2=v2']`

More info: https://nodejs.org/api/http.html#messageheaders

comments.author: mkhani01
comments.body:
After literally light‑years of debugging I finally discovered that Android’s OkHttp **will not** fetch missing intermediates the way iOS or desktop browsers do. My server was only ever serving the leaf certificate, so every HTTPS call on Android instantly failed with `ERR_NETWORK`.

**The fix is 100% Nginx‑side**—no application‑level hacks needed:

1. **Build a true full‑chain bundle**  
   Concatenate your leaf cert plus all intermediate certs into one file:
 
```bash
   cat /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.crt \
       /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.ca-bundle \
     > /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt
```


Verify you now have two or more certificates in it:

```bash
grep -c "BEGIN CERTIFICATE" /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt
# → should print 2+
```

2. **Point Nginx at the full‑chain**
   In your SSL server block, reference the new bundle:

   ```nginx
   server {
     listen 443 ssl;
     server_name <YOUR_DOMAIN> www.<YOUR_DOMAIN>;

     ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>_fullchain.crt;
     ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/ssl/<YOUR_DOMAIN>.key;

     # …your proxy_pass and other config…
   }
   ```

3. **Test & reload Nginx**

   ```bash
   nginx -t && nginx -s reload
   ```

4. **Confirm the chain**

   ```bash
   openssl s_client -connect <YOUR_DOMAIN>:443 -showcerts
   ```

   You should see both your leaf **and** intermediate(s) listed, ending with:

   ```
   Verify return code: 0 (ok)
   ```

Once Android sees the complete chain, OkHttp will happily complete the TLS handshake and your HTTPS requests will succeed on **both** iOS and Android.

```
::contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
```

title: Server-Side Request Forgery Vulnerability (CVE-2024-39338)
security_topic: remediation version for SSRF vulnerability
qa_summary: Whether a fix is available for the SSRF vulnerability described in CVE-2024-39338 and which version (v1.7.4) resolves it.

comments.author: jeffhacks
comments.body:
### Describe the bug

Axios is vulnerable to a Server-Side Request Forgery attack caused by unexpected behaviour where requests for path relative URLS gets processed as protocol relative URLs.

This could be leveraged by an attacker to perform arbitrary requests from the server, potentially accessing internal systems or exfiltrating sensitive data.

### To Reproduce

In this vulnerable code snippet, the developer intended to invoke a path relative to the base URL, however it allows an attacker to craft a malicious protocol-relative URL which is then requested by the server. Given protocol-relative URLs are not relevant server-side as there is no protocol to be relative to, the expected result would be an error. Instead, a valid URL is produced and requested.

Example Vulnerable Code
```typescript
const axios = require('axios');

this.axios = axios.create({
  baseURL: 'https://userapi.example.com',
});

//userId = '12345';
userId = '/google.com'

this.axios.get(`/${userId}`).then(function (response) {
  console.log(`config.baseURL:  ${response.config.baseURL}`);
  console.log(`config.method:   ${response.config.method}`);
  console.log(`config.url:      ${response.config.url}`);
  console.log(`res.responseUrl: ${response.request.res.responseUrl}`);
});
```

Expected Output (Prior to axios 1.3.2):
```typescript
(node:10243) UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning: TypeError [ERR_INVALID_URL]: Invalid URL: //example.org
```

Developer might also have expected:
```yaml
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      https://userapi.example.com//www.google.com/
res.responseUrl: https://userapi.example.com//www.google.com/
```

Observed Output:
```yaml
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      //google.com
res.responseUrl: http://www.google.com/
```

This behaviour is potentially unexpected and introduces the potential for attackers to request URLs on arbitrary hosts other than the host in the base URL.

The code related to parsing and preparing the URL for server-side requests, prior to version 1.3.2, only passed one argument to the Node.js URL class.
```typescript
    const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url);
    const parsed = new URL(fullPath);
    const protocol = parsed.protocol || supportedProtocols[0];
```

Version 1.3.2 introduced `http://localhost` as a base URL for relative paths (https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/5458)
```typescript
    const fullPath = buildFullPath(config.baseURL, config.url);
    const parsed = new URL(fullPath, 'http://localhost');
    const protocol = parsed.protocol || supportedProtocols[0];
```

As protocol-relative URLs are considered to be absolute, the config.baseURL value is ignored so protocol-relative URLs are passed to the URL class without a protocol. The node.js URL class will then prepend the protocol from `'http://localhost'` to the protocol-relative URL.

For example
```typescript
> new URL('//google.com', 'https://example.org');
URL {
  href: 'https://google.com/',
  ...
}

> new URL('//google.com', 'file://example.org');
URL {
  href: 'file://google.com/',
  ...
}
```

### Code snippet

_No response_

### Expected behavior

An error could be raised when attempting to request protocol-relative URLs server-side as unlike in a client-side browser session, there is no established protocol to be relative to.

comments.author: SilverSting
comments.body:
Hi. Trying to understand this vulnerability better.

**Mixed use of relative and absolute (including, protocol-relative) URLs**

Axios will see `//google.com` as an argument to `get` call, since the text substitution will occur outside of the function call and that's an acceptable value, isn't it? It's quite possible that the same client instance could be used for fetching both relative URL and absolute URL based resources.
```
userId = '/google.com'
this.axios.get(`/${userId}`);
```

Of course this may not align with application developer's expectation (ie. to be relative path). But it feels like that's not Axios' problem to solve. Axios could potentially warn this use pattern (ie. use of baseUrl with non relative path), but it seems too harsh for axios to dictate this.

**Impact of using protocol-relative URLs**

The following code kinda forces `http` protocol if protocol-relative URLs are used. 
```
const parsed = new URL(fullPath, 'http://localhost');
```

Is this the main concern here? I guess an attacker could potentially move away from non-http protocol (eg. local file location, deemed safe) to http protocol to deliver remotely located malicious files into the target system.

**Expected behavior**

>An error could be raised when attempting to request protocol-relative URLs server-side as unlike in a client-side browser session, there is no established protocol to be relative to.

If this is indeed a good solution, then `isAbsoluteURL` could be updated to ignore protocol-relative URLs to produce this output. Please note `config.url` is set by the `_request` [implementation,](https://github.com/axios/axios/blob/c6cce43cd94489f655f4488c5a50ecaf781c94f2/lib/core/Axios.js#L65), so it will be still `//google.com`. But requested url will be **combined** url.

```
config.baseURL:  https://userapi.example.com
config.method:   get
config.url:      //google.com
res.responseUrl: https://userapi.example.com//google.com
```

>

The problem here isn't necessarily the behaviour of axios in the browser, it's the behaviour of it in a server-side context where the server is making requests from a private network.

As the report says, in a server-side context, there is no base protocol for a protocol-relative URL to be relative to. Therefore, a protocol-relative URL should not be considered valid in that context.

How the attack could be constructed is sort of secondary to that. If it doesn't make sense in that context, we should disallow it.

title: CI: consider adding npm dependency caching to setup-node step
security_topic: CI cache pollution risk assessment
qa_summary: Whether adding npm dependency caching to the CI workflow introduces a risk of cache pollution and what the project's permissions and documentation regarding lockfiles dictate.

comments.author: eddieteall
comments.body:
I was exploring the CI workflow as part of my university project on GitHub Actions and noticed that the setup-node step doesn't currently include dependency caching.

The current setup-node step looks like this:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'

Adding cache: 'npm' would allow GitHub Actions to cache node_modules between runs, which can reduce install time on repeated builds:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'
    cache: 'npm'

I tested this on my own Node.js project and it worked without any other changes needed. I appreciate this may already be a considered decision, so happy to hear if there's a reason it's been left out.

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
I looked at the history and caching is not mentioned anywhere in #5599, which reworked the CI. The older Appveyor CI did [cache `node_modules`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c96c690dc087d121137c97318215e03a432395c5/appveyor.yml#L22-L23), so maybe everyone just missed this.

The "Install dependencies" step does not take a lot of time (7-15 seconds on ubuntu runners; 20+ on windows), but I think it's enough for cache to make it faster. GitHub only stores cache for [7 days](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy:~:text=GitHub%20will%20remove%20any%20cache%20entries%20that%20have%20not%20been%20accessed%20in%20over%207%20days%2E) and there have been periods when CI did not run for more than this[^1]. Saving cache will make the execution time a bit longer, but in my opinion it is not something that we should care about.

Finally, cache can allow compromising CI though cache pollution (evict cache and then make GitHub save your version with malicious additions, which will then be used to install dependencies). This is also not a problem for us, because running actions requires maintainer approval (though I'm not completely sure about this) and workflows that could use cache ([ci](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L16-L17) and [legacy](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/legacy.yml#L18-L19)) have read-only [`contents` permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#permissions).

[^1]: Adding [scheduled runs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) would allow avoiding cache expiry and, more importantly, help us faster detect regressions caused by dependency updates.

comments.author: gabrieel1007

comments.body:
In this case, the reported vulnerability in `qs` (CVE-2025-15284) is already addressed by default in Express. Current Express releases depend on patched versions of `qs`:

- **Express 4** specifies `"qs": "~6.14.0"`, which resolves to `>=6.14.0 <6.15.0` and therefore pulls in the patched `6.14.1` release by default. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f62378e1bc776259c0a471476c2dc043a02ac762/package.json#L56

- **Express 5** specifies `"qs": "^6.14.0"`, which also pulls in the patched versions automatically. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c2fb76e99f7379b706a5510b4b2dd08a1b710b7b/package.json#L55

As a result, users installing Express without overriding dependency resolutions already receive a version of `qs` that includes the fix, and the reported issue does not represent an unpatched vulnerability in Express itself.

title: location function does not validate potentially malicious URLs

comments.author: xzyingxiashubro
SantiagoCecena
comments.body:
Hi,

I'm interested in working on this issue.

The current behavior of `res.location()` allowing `javascript:` or `data:` schemes in the `Location` header poses a significant **XSS vulnerability**, as browsers might execute such malicious URLs. While `encodeUrl` handles URL encoding, it doesn't validate the safety of the URL scheme itself.

I'd like to propose adding a **scheme validation** step within the `res.location` function. This would involve checking if the provided URL starts with safe schemes like `http://`, `https://`, or is a relative path (`/`). Any other schemes (e.g., `javascript:`, `data:`) would be rejected or handled safely to prevent this type of attack.

I believe this enhancement would significantly improve the **default security of Express** for all users.

Would it be possible for me to pick this up and submit a pull request? I'm happy to discuss the implementation details further.

Thanks,
Santiago

Furthermore, there are perfectly valid use cases for non http schemes in location headers.

title: res.redirect cannot carry the request header I set
security_topic: HTTP redirection header security implications
qa_summary: Whether custom request headers are preserved during a redirect and the security implications of removing headers like Authorization and Cookie as defined in RFC 9110.

comments.author: YJGGZHK
comments.body: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/91c14e66-f7ce-4046-9b14-df73beda90f2)

comments.author: YJGGZHK
comments.body:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/30a7972c-ed24-4b6b-875a-3795fcfbb8ae)
I can ensure that the id is set in the header before forwarding

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
Do you want to:

1. perform (or not) a redirect when a certain header is set,
2. remove a header from redirected request, or
3. add a header to redirected request?

1\. is easy:

```js
app.use((req, res, next) => {
    // redirect if id header is truthy
    if (req.headers.id) res.redirect('https://...');
    else next();
}
```

2\. and 3. as far as I know are impossible. Redirections are described in RFC 9110 in section [15.4. _Redirection 3xx_](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.3xx). The RFC says (emphasis mine):
> When automatically following a redirected request, **the user agent SHOULD resend the original request message** with the following modifications:
>
> 1. Replace the target URI with the URI referenced by the redirection response's [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field value after resolving it relative to the original request's target URI.
> 2. Remove header fields that were automatically generated by the implementation, replacing them with updated values as appropriate to the new request. This includes:
>    1. (...)
> 3. Consider removing header fields that were not automatically generated by the implementation (i.e., those present in the request because they were added by the calling context) where there are security implications; this includes but is not limited to [Authorization](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.authorization) and Cookie.
> 4. Change the request method according to the redirecting status code's semantics, if applicable.
> 5. If the request method has been changed to GET or HEAD, remove content-specific header fields, including (but not limited to) [Content-Encoding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-encoding), [Content-Language](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-language), [Content-Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-location), [Content-Type](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-type), [Content-Length](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-length), Digest, [Last-Modified](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.last-modified).

In general, the user agent (e.g. browser) sends the original request, but changes some necessary automatically generated headers (e.g. `Host`) and **removes headers that may have security implications such as `Authorization` and `Cookie`**. The list of removed headers will probably depend on the user agent - [here is the list from Firefox](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/6cc05c6620814bf3eb05278ccf3b1f49690b7740/netwerk/protocol/http/HttpBaseChannel.cpp#123-148).\
The RFC does not offer a way of adding or removing custom headers when redirecting a request - whatever was in the original request is in the redirected one (with the exceptions mentioned above).

comments.author: YJGGZHK

human_note: he question is a viable security question because it asks whether HTTP redirects can preserve or alter request headers in a way that impacts security-sensitive headers (e.g., Authorization, Cookie), and the answer directly addresses redirect security behavior defined in RFC 9110.

comments.body:
We will be recommending folks use a more robust input validation approach for this. If you want, here is the open api library I maintain: https://github.com/wesleytodd/express-openapi/

The reason for this is mainly security around DOS protection. There is no way to support path segment regular expression matching while also avoiding major performance regressions. See more here: https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/

This is a 100% big win for the ecosystem longer term, as regular expression route matching was one of the worst decisions from the early days which has stuck around. > This is why I am hesitant do add an action for this as I would rather ask GitHub for better spam management tooling.

Agree with @wesleytodd. The issue is quite complex because the moderation in GitHub is not an easy thing:
- Many people (those that are watching the repo) will receive a notification in their email or in the app/web once a new PR is created. This will occur even before a Github Action is triggered.

There are other scenarios that are less frequent but more prone to use GitHub Actions to moderate, for example when people do comments that include offensive content or heavily language. In most projects that I am involved the moderation is done by the humans behind the project or a specific team that volunteer to do it, it is a heavy job. title: Can express req.headers[x] be an array?
security_topic: array values in request headers for Express/Node.js
qa_summary: The developer needed to know whether Express can include array‑valued headers such as set‑cookie and how to safely combine them, and the answer cites the Node.js HTTP documentation (https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders) which states that only the set‑cookie header is an array and should not be merged into a string.

comments.author: RobertSandiford
dougwilson
comments.body:
Hello, so the `req.headers` object is just from Node.js HTTP itself; Express.js doesn't set anything there. This means the rules are types are that of the version of Node.js you are running on. Here is their documentation:

https://nodejs.org/dist/latest-v21.x/docs/api/http.html#messageheaders

And notably I see this about array values:

> set-cookie is always an array. Duplicates are added to the array.

I don't think `set-cookie` can be safely combined into a string, which is why it seems the only one that Node.js will put as an array.

I hope that helps.

Edit: also, it is pretty much non-existent that `set-cookie` header would even be in a request to a server like express, as that is a response header, not a request header.

human_note: Accepted because the question is about header typing and runtime behavior in Express/Node, which is valid framework-level behavior. The answer is valid since it correctly states that Express does not transform headers (they come from Node.js), and accurately identifies that set-cookie is the only header that Node may represent as an array in req.headers, while also correctly noting it is primarily a response header rather than a request header.

title: Basic auth `realm` is REQUIRED but handled as optional
security_topic: compliance of basic auth realm with RFC specifications
qa_summary: Whether the 'realm' parameter in Basic auth is required for RFC compliance, with the answer citing RFC 7235 and RFC 7617.

comments.author: tvogel
comments.body:
According to https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 , specification of the `realm` parameter is REQUIRED, so making `realm` optional here

https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/blob/643d2845de09a437b955a163ab25eb0887bfd0e1/fastapi/security/http.py#L195

and at related places, is misleading and makes it easy to create non-conforming APIs. It bit me when a Shelly device refused (rightfully) to authenticate against the API which was using the default (missing) `realm` behavior.

comments.author: tvogel
comments.body: Ah, good that this is already in the works! However, the fix to default it to "global" is questionable to me because that is a string that in general gets presented to users as a prompt to provide credentials, so shouldn't have a rather meaningless default. A good framework should make the framework user provide relevant detail like the realm. If they use basic auth, they need to define a realm.

comments.author: YuriiMotov
comments.body:
I think we should close this issue.

As Sebastian mentioned in [this comment](https://github.com/fastapi/fastapi/pull/13786#pullrequestreview-3501695067), `realm` seems to be not required in latest version of RFC.

> I also noted that the spec says that the realm is now optional, but only in a footer note (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A). 😂 Anyway, we are good with that now.


I checked this and agree:

The https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7617#autoid-3 states:

> The authentication parameter 'realm' is REQUIRED ([RFC7235], Section 2.2).

But if we go to Section 2.2 of RFC7235, we have:

> [2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2.2).  Protection Space (Realm)
> 
>    The "realm" authentication parameter is reserved for use by
>    authentication schemes that wish to indicate a scope of protection.
> 
>    A protection space is defined by the canonical root URI (the scheme
>    and authority components of the effective request URI; see [Section](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)
>    [5.5 of [RFC7230]](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-5.5)) of the server being accessed, **in combination with**
>    **the realm value if present.** ...

So, current version of RFC7235 doesn't say that `realm` is required.

Moreover, it's mentioned in [Appendix A](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#appendix-A):

>    The "realm" parameter is no longer always required on challenges;
>    consequently, the ABNF allows challenges without any auth parameters.
>    ([Section 2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-2))

human_note: Standards interpretation issue affecting HTTP Basic authentication behavior (realm optionality, RFC 7235 vs RFC 7617 evolution)

title: HTTPBearer security scheme is returning 403 instead or 401
security_topic: HTTP status code for unauthenticated requests
qa_summary: Whether the HTTPBearer security scheme should return a 401 or 403 status code for unauthenticated requests, with the answer anchored in RFC 6750.

comments.author: Kludex
comments.body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/discussions/9130
Originally posted by **aaaaahaaaaa** September 8, 2020 HTTPBearer security scheme enabled as a dependency is returning a `403` when a request is unauthenticated because of a missing or a malformed `authorization` header. In those scenarios, a `401` should be returned instead.
## Related PRs - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/2120 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/5310 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/5332 - https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/pull/9312

comments.author: ordinary-jamie
comments.body:
Hey @Kludex, what do you think about raising a `HTTP 400 BAD REQUEST` for cases where the authentication scheme is not correctly 'bearer'?

[From RFC 6750 Section 3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6750#section-3.1):

```
invalid_request
         The request is missing a required parameter, includes an
         unsupported parameter or parameter value, repeats the same
         parameter, uses more than one method for including an access
         token, or is otherwise malformed.  The resource server SHOULD
         respond with the HTTP 400 (Bad Request) status code.

invalid_token
         The access token provided is expired, revoked, malformed, or
         invalid for other reasons.  The resource SHOULD respond with
         the HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) status code.  The client MAY
         request a new access token and retry the protected resource
         request.
```

My reading of this text is that:

- when the server understands the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is correct) but the token itself is malformed we should return a `401`
- when the server does **not** understand the request (i.e. 'bearer' scheme is wrong), then we should return a `400`

comments.author: ordinary-jamie
comments.body:
[`fastapi/security/http.py` L#125](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/master/fastapi/security/http.py#L125-L130)

EDIT: Wrong line sorry

comments.body:
Sorry, my misunderstanding. At any rate, I don't think it is necessary after reading section 3 again I realised they offered an example for this scenario.

**tldr; 401 seems like the appropriate error code 👍** 

```
 If the request lacks any authentication information (e.g., the client
   was unaware that authentication is necessary or attempted using an
   unsupported authentication method), the resource server SHOULD NOT
   include an error code or other error information.

   For example:

     HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
     WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example"
```

Would probably be good if that could be straightened out for all occurrences there.

comments.author: sehraramiz
comments.body:
[Dependant](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L15) object has a cache_key attribute which the dependency resolver of fastapi uses it to cache dependencies and use the already resolved dependencies (get_session in this case).
according to [this line](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/63a5ffcf577abc6015d021f65857b3826d8db74e/fastapi/dependencies/models.py#L58) of Dependant class the cache_key is generated using the **dependency function reference** and **security scopes**.
when you use get_authenticated_user as a security dependency every param in get_authenticated_user gets the security scopes of the parent api (user_activate).
so when resloving dependencies from user_activate with scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ('activate'))```
when resloving dependencies from user_activate with no scopes, the param ```session: Session = Depends(get_session)``` gets saved in dependency_cache with a key like ```(<function get_session at 0x7fb87827c9d0>, ())```

i think this behavior might be a security feature.

it might help you to read [this part of the doc](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/sub-dependencies/?h=dependenc#using-the-same-dependency-multiple-times) on dependency cache

comments.body:
@araujo88 you can ref this issue: https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/issues/394

in summary it is a bug or design issue from starlette, and there is work around:

```python
from typing import Mapping

from starlette.requests import Request

from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter, Depends

app = FastAPI()
api_router = APIRouter()

@api_router.post("/")
def read_root(arg: Mapping[str, str]):
    return {"Hello": "World"}

async def auth_middleware(request: Request):
    # you can implement your auth here
    print(await request.json())

# the trick here is including auth_middleware in the dependencies:
app.include_router(api_router, dependencies=[Depends(auth_middleware)])
```
thus this middleware logic will work on every requests, we use it same way in our production env, works fine.

note: `Dependencies` will inject your auth logic into each request, for more detail ref: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/

comments.author: leo-aa88

comments.author: xingdongzhe
comments.body:
@araujo88 It can't be using `self.stream()`, for per request, only one time can use `self.stream()`.  
Or you will hang forever because of `await self.event_message.wait()`  
[You can see here: uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543](https://github.com/encode/uvicorn/blob/fedf67e68d3f81c846bf3740c8ae21fa133000a4/uvicorn/protocols/http/h11_impl.py#L543)  
This is because that when `self.stream()` done, there are no action to notify `self.event_message`
This `asyncio.Event` will be notified of four actions:
- when Connection Lost
- when body_data received
- when body_data readed done
- when write reponse data done

And you can try this:
```
async for chunk in request.stream():
    print(chunk)
await request.json()
```

comments.body: If you want to keep using BaseHTTPMiddleware, I would suggest you create a new Request object at the end of your middleware to avoid such indefinite waits.

I guess that he meant that yellow warning sign.
If you use `SameSite=none`, it is required to set `secure` attribute aswell as described [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie/SameSite).

```py3
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/home")

    response.set_cookie(key="foo", value="bar", secure=False, samesite="lax")

creds = Credentials(password="helloworld")

a = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(a)  # {'password': '**********'}, as expected
b = jsonable_encoder(creds, custom_encoder=ENCODERS)
print(b)  # {'password': 'helloworld'}, as expected
c = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(c)  # gives {'password': 'helloworld'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?


creds = Credentials(password="123456789")

d = jsonable_encoder(creds)
print(d)  # gives {'password': '123456789'}, but should be {'password': '**********'}?
```


### Description

* I'm using `jsonable_encoder` at multiple locations in the code, sometimes with `custom_encoder` and sometimes without.
* My understanding is that passing `custom_encoder` should only affect the current call and not modify any global state.
* What actually happens is that it modifies `__config__.json_encoders`, and as a result, public API endpoints might suddenly start returning secret values that should be filtered.

0.78.0
